finishQuestions.why: The surface decides the product family before anything else: a wall, a ceiling and a steel gate do not share a coating.
Condition decides the preparation, and whether a primer or a screeding pass is needed before any finish coat.

finishQuestions.prompt: How much wear will it take?
finishQuestions.why: Wear decides between a flat film that hides imperfections and a tighter film that can be washed.

finishQuestions.prompt: How do you want it to look?
finishQuestions.why: Sheen changes how the colour reads: matt scatters light and looks deeper, silk returns light and looks richer.

prepSituations.label: New render or blockwork
signs: Grey, unpainted cement
The building is weeks or months old, not years
Hairline shrinkage cracks as it cures

steps.detail: Cement render cures by chemical reaction, not by drying. 14 days is the absolute minimum; 28 days wherever the schedule allows. Painting early traps moisture and alkali behind the film.
Tape a square of clear polythene tight to the wall for 24 hours. Condensation on the underside means the wall is still releasing water — wait.

steps.step: Level it if it needs it
steps.detail: Where the blockwork undulates, apply two thin passes of screeding compound, sanded at 120 grit between passes. Fill with compound, never with a thick coat of paint.
Wipe down with a damp cloth and allow to dry. A surface that feels chalky to the hand will not hold paint.
One full coat of alkali-resisting primer on everything new or repaired. It blocks alkali burn and equalises porosity so the topcoat draws evenly.
Two full coats of the chosen finish, recoating at the interval on the data sheet. In the rainy season expect that interval to lengthen.

warnings: New render under 14 days old should not be painted at all — the blistering appears weeks later and no topcoat repairs it.

prepSituations.label: Previously painted and sound
signs: The existing film is firmly attached
No cracking, no lifting at edges
Colour is faded or dirty rather than failing

steps.detail: Warm water with a little detergent, working from the bottom up so dirty runs do not streak dry paint. Rinse and allow to dry fully.
Key any glossy area so the new coat has something to hold. Sand back to a dull surface, then dust off.
Fill nail holes and small damage, sand flat, and spot-prime every bare or filled patch — an unprimed patch drinks the topcoat and reads as a dull spot.
Going significantly lighter or deeper needs an extra coat. A dark colour over a light one may need a tinted primer; ask the desk.
Two full coats, cutting in the edges first and rolling from a wet edge so no lap lines dry into the film.

warnings: Do not mix two finishes on one wall — the join reads as a patch in raking light.

prepSituations.label: Flaking or peeling paint
signs: Coating lifting in flakes or sheets
Edges you can pick at with a fingernail
Bare plaster showing through

steps.step: Strip back to a sound edge
steps.detail: Scrape and sand until nothing lifts. Feather the edge so the step between old film and bare substrate cannot be felt, let alone seen.
Flaking is usually moisture behind the film, or painting over a chalky surface. If the wall is damp, treat the damp first — recoating over it reproduces the failure.
Remove every particle of scraped paint and dust. Adhesion fails on dust more often than on anything else.
One full coat of primer over every exposed substrate, not a dabbed-on spot coat.

steps.step: Fill if the surface is uneven
steps.detail: Where scraping has left hollows, screed, sand and re-prime before finishing.
Two full coats over the whole wall, not only the repaired area, so the sheen is even.

warnings: Painting over a flaking film bonds to the loose layer, not the wall. The new coat lifts with the old one.

prepSituations.label: Uneven, pitted or badly patched
signs: Visible undulations in raking light
Holes, chased conduits, old fixings
Patch repairs that shine against the rest

steps.step: Find the worst of it with raking light
steps.detail: A torch held along the wall shows every hollow. Mark them: a flat finish will not hide them and a silk finish will exaggerate them.
Damp the wall down first so it does not pull water from the mix. Apply 1–2 mm with a steel trowel, allow to set, then apply a second thin pass to close the surface.
Sand between and after the passes, then dust off completely.
Screeded surface is porous and must be primed before the topcoat, or the finish goes patchy.
A flat finish forgives what is left; a silk finish demands the surface be genuinely flat. If the wall cannot be made flat, choose matt.

warnings: A thick coat of paint is not a filler. It shrinks, cracks and shows the hollow underneath.

prepSituations.label: Chalky or powdering surface
signs: Colour comes off on your palm
Weathered exterior paint
A powdery film over old render

steps.detail: Rub the surface with your hand or a dark cloth. If pigment transfers, the binder has failed and no topcoat will hold without a sealing coat.
Remove as much loose material as you can by brushing, then wash down and allow to dry completely.
Treat with a stabilising wash or primer and allow it to dry fully. On chalky exterior render a bonding agent is the right call.
Rub again after the stabiliser has cured. If pigment still lifts, treat it again — do not proceed to a finish coat.
Two coats of a breathable exterior system on facades; two coats of the chosen interior finish inside.

warnings: A wall that feels chalky to the hand will not hold paint. Stabilise it or strip it; there is no third option.

prepSituations.label: Damp wall or tide mark
signs: A darker band rising from the floor
Blistering or a musty smell
Paint lifting without flaking, plaster softening

steps.detail: Most damp comes from one of four places: a failed roof or gutter, a bridged damp-proof course, plumbing leakage, or rising moisture in a wall built off the ground. Trace the tide mark upward and look for the highest point of wetness.
Repair the roof, the gutter, the leak or the ground path. This is a building job, not a painting job, and it comes first.
Ventilate and wait. Use the polythene test: tape a square tight to the wall for 24 hours and look for condensation on the underside.
Strip blown or powdery coating back to sound substrate, and remove salt-contaminated plaster where necessary.
Once the wall is genuinely dry: prime, fill, and apply two coats. Photograph the wall first, so you have a reference for what normal looks like.

warnings: No coating, at any price, will stop rising damp. If the cause is structural, fix the structure — paint comes after.
Never seal an actively damp wall with gloss or a waterproof sealer. The film blisters from behind.

prepSituations.label: Mould, mildew or algae
signs: Black or green speckling
Usually at corners, behind furniture or under a window
A bathroom, a kitchen or a shaded exterior wall

steps.detail: Mould needs water and a food source. Increase ventilation, fix leaks and move furniture off cold walls — otherwise it returns within weeks of repainting.
Use a proprietary wash, follow its instructions, and allow the surface to dry thoroughly. Do not dry-brush live mould into the air.
Once treated and dry, wash down to remove the staining and any remaining film.
One coat of primer over the treated area so the finish draws evenly.
Two coats of a finish carrying an anti-fungi additive — the Matt and Silk lines both carry one.

warnings: An anti-fungi additive protects the paint film. It does not remove moisture from the room, so ventilation and leak repair still matter.

prepSituations.label: Salt bloom (efflorescence)
signs: White, powdery patches or crystals
Returns a few weeks after being painted over
Usually on new or damp masonry

steps.step: Do not wash it into the wall
steps.detail: Efflorescence is soluble salt carried to the surface by water. Wetting it dissolves it back into the substrate, where it crystallises again.
Stiff brush, dry surface, and remove as much of the bloom as you can.
The salt only travels when water moves. Until the source is fixed, the bloom returns through any coating.
Apply a stabilising wash and allow the wall to dry completely — verified with the polythene test, not with a guess.
One full coat of alkali-resisting primer, then two finish coats.

warnings: Painting over salt bloom guarantees the paint lifts in sheets, taking the salt with it.

prepSituations.label: Old gloss on timber or metal
signs: A hard, shiny film on a door, frame or gate
Yellowed or cracked with age
Bare timber or rust showing at edges

steps.step: Strip the loose, keep the sound
steps.detail: Remove anything lifting, then sand the rest back to a dull, keyed surface. A gloss film that is sound can be overcoated; one that is cracking cannot.
Degrease with a solvent wipe and treat rust back to bright metal before applying a metal primer.
Sand with the grain, seal the knots, and apply a wood primer.
Remove every trace of dust and solvent, and let the surface dry before coating.
Two thin coats beat one thick one. Brush in the direction of the grain or the length of the steel, and observe the 16-hour recoat interval.

warnings: Gloss is solvent-based: ventilate the space and use the PPE the data sheet specifies.

prepSituations.label: Coastal or salt-air exposure
signs: A facade near the creek or the sea
Salt crusting on metalwork
Faster chalking and fading than inland

steps.detail: Salt air and UV accelerate chalking and corrosion. Plan a wash-down and an inspection every year rather than waiting for failure.
Remove deposited salt by washing; coating over salt reproduces efflorescence under the film.
Treat any rust back to bright metal and prime it before it spreads under a sound-looking film.
Prime, then two coats of the textured exterior coating, which bridges hairline cracks and sheds water.
Keep the elevation out of rain for 24 hours after the final coat, and avoid painting in direct midday sun on a hot wall.

warnings: If you can feel heat radiating from the render, wait. A hot wall flash-dries a water-based coat before it can be laid off.
